meta.blurb: Noah rides a bicycle for a living and wants to feel lighter and stronger. His neighbour Ines studies microbes, and she shows him the tiny world inside every gut, and how everyday food can help it thrive.
meta.bible: Noah: a young bicycle courier of about twenty-eight who eats quick meals on the road and wants to understand his gut; honest, hungry and a little impatient. Ines: his neighbour, a Microbiologist at a university, who studies microbes; patient, funny, and careful to say what science does not yet know. The story runs over about six weeks in a city, in Noah's flat, Ines's laboratory and a street market. Key terms: Gut, Small intestine, Large intestine, Colon, Microbes, Bacteria, Microbiome, Fibre, Prebiotics, Probiotics, Resistant starch, Polyphenols, Fermentation, Fermented foods, Short-chain fatty acids, Butyrate, Antibiotics, Constipation, Diarrhoea, Irritable bowel syndrome, Registered dietitian. Facts: the gut is several metres long; the large intestine holds most gut microbes; by recent estimates the body holds about as many microbes as human cells; microbes ferment fibre into short-chain fatty acids that feed the cells lining the colon, and they also make gas; many national guides advise about thirty grams of fibre a day for adults and most adults eat less; a large citizen-science survey found that people who ate more than thirty kinds of plant a week had a more varied set of gut microbes than people who ate ten or fewer, which is a link and not proof; a small university trial found that ten weeks of eating more fermented foods increased the variety of gut microbes; antibiotics save lives but also disturb gut microbes, and should be taken only when a doctor prescribes them. Foods: Beans, Lentils, Oats, Barley, Brown rice, Onions, Garlic, Leeks, Bananas, Yoghurt, Kefir, Kimchi, Sauerkraut, Miso. Safety facts: add fibre slowly and drink water; see a doctor for blood in the stool, black stools, unexplained weight loss, ongoing pain or a lasting change in bowel habits; people with bowel conditions, allergies, a pregnancy, a child to feed or on medicine should ask a doctor or registered dietitian; do not cut out gluten before testing for coeliac disease; home-made fermented food needs clean jars and should be thrown away if it smells bad or grows mould. This book is general information and is not medical advice. Voice and tone: warm, clear and a little funny; honest about uncertainty; no invented numbers, studies or quotes; no diagnosis and no personal treatment advice.

beats.scene: Noah eats a quick sandwich on a bicycle at a red traffic light
beats.summary: Noah, a bicycle courier, eats quick meals on the road and wonders what they do inside him.

beats.scene: Ines points at a microscope in a bright university laboratory
beats.summary: His neighbour Ines studies microbes at a university and offers to explain the tiny world inside the gut.

beats.scene: Ines draws a long winding tube on a whiteboard with a marker
beats.summary: The gut is a long tube, several metres in length, running from the mouth to the end of the body.

beats.scene: A small cartoon of tiny bacteria crowded together inside a long tube
beats.summary: Most gut microbes live in the large intestine, and the body holds about as many microbes as human cells.

beats.scene: Ines holds up a jar of green liquid with a label that reads Microbiome
beats.summary: The microbiome is the whole community of microbes in the gut, and each person's community is different.

beats.scene: A friendly microbe waves while a spiky germ is pushed away by a crowd
beats.summary: Most microbes are harmless or helpful, and a crowd of good ones helps to keep harmful germs away.

beats.scene: Ines draws four small arrows pointing away from a gut on a whiteboard
beats.summary: Gut microbes help to digest food, make some vitamins and train the immune system.

beats.scene: Glowing dots join a head and a gut like a long telephone cable
beats.summary: The gut and brain talk through nerves, hormones and immune signals, and early research suggests food may affect mood, though much is unknown.

beats.scene: A bowl of beans and oats with tiny cartoon microbes eating from it
beats.summary: Microbes feed on the parts of food that we cannot digest, mostly fibre.

beats.scene: A wheat stalk, a carrot and an apple lie beside a ruler
beats.summary: Fibre is the part of plant foods that we cannot digest; it comes in different kinds, such as the soluble and insoluble kinds.

beats.scene: Ines drops a spoon into bubbling oatmeal to show a gel forming
beats.summary: Microbes ferment fibre into short-chain fatty acids, which feed the cells lining the large intestine and may help to calm inflammation.

beats.scene: A measuring bar shows thirty grams next to a small bowl of cereal
beats.summary: Many national guides advise about thirty grams of fibre a day for adults, and most adults eat less.

beats.scene: Noah writes numbers in a notebook beside a crisp packet and a sandwich
beats.summary: Noah checks the fibre in his usual week and finds that he eats far less than the guides suggest.

beats.scene: Noah adds beans to a plate beside a tall glass of water
beats.summary: Fibre should be increased slowly over weeks, with plenty of water, so the gut can adjust.

beats.scene: A cartoon bubble of air rises from a pot of beans on a stove
beats.summary: Wind is a normal result of microbes fermenting fibre, and most people pass wind many times a day.

beats.scene: A tin of beans being rinsed under a tap in a colander
beats.summary: Beans and lentils are rich in fibre, and starting with small portions, and rinsing tinned beans, helps the gut to adapt.

beats.scene: A wooden bowl of oats beside brown rice and pearl barley in jars
beats.summary: Whole grains such as oats, barley and brown rice keep their fibre, and oats and barley contain a fibre called beta-glucan.

beats.scene: Noah bites into a crunchy apple with the skin on beside carrots
beats.summary: Fruit and vegetables bring fibre, and eating the skins where safe adds more; different ones feed different microbes.

beats.scene: A small pile of seeds and nuts beside a jar of chia and flax
beats.summary: Nuts and seeds add fibre and healthy fats; ground or soaked seeds are easier to digest, and nut allergies are serious.

beats.scene: Ines hands Noah a paper with a list of plant names in colours
beats.summary: Variety matters because different microbes like different fibres, and a varied diet feeds a more varied community.

beats.scene: A bar chart on a screen compares two groups of people
beats.summary: A large survey found that people eating more than thirty kinds of plant a week had a more varied gut community, though this is a link, not proof.

beats.scene: Noah ticks plant names on a fridge chart beside a jar of oats
beats.summary: Noah starts a weekly plant count; herbs, spices, nuts and seeds all count as different plants.

beats.scene: A tropical rainforest and a bare field of one crop shown side by side
beats.summary: A varied microbiome is generally linked with better health, much like a rainforest is more resilient than a single-crop field.

beats.scene: Garlic, leeks, onions and asparagus laid out beside a green banana on a board
beats.summary: Prebiotics are fibres that feed helpful microbes; onions, garlic, leeks, oats and slightly green bananas contain them.

beats.scene: A cooled bowl of boiled potatoes, rice and pasta in a fridge
beats.summary: Resistant starch survives digestion and feeds microbes; cooked and cooled potatoes, rice and pasta, and slightly green bananas contain more of it.

beats.scene: Purple cabbage, blueberries, green tea and dark chocolate in a row
beats.summary: Polyphenols are colourful plant substances; gut microbes change them into other substances, and research on their effects is promising but young.

beats.scene: Kimchi, sauerkraut, kefir and yoghurt jars on a shelf in a market stall
beats.summary: Fermented foods such as yoghurt, kefir, kimchi, sauerkraut and miso contain live microbes, and some of them may help the gut.

beats.scene: Ines points to a chart of rising bars on a laboratory wall
beats.summary: A small university study found that ten weeks of eating more fermented foods increased the variety of gut microbes.

beats.scene: Ines and Noah read a shelf of pill bottles labelled probiotic in a pharmacy
beats.summary: Probiotic supplements have mixed evidence; some help in particular conditions, but the effect is usually short-lived and not a substitute for a varied diet.

beats.scene: Noah packs cabbage into a clean glass jar with salt on a kitchen counter
beats.summary: Home fermenting is simple but needs clean jars and salt, and anything that smells bad or grows mould should be thrown away.

beats.scene: A doctor hands a small box of tablets labelled antibiotics to Noah's sister
beats.summary: Antibiotics save lives but also disturb gut microbes; take them only when a doctor prescribes them and follow the instructions.

beats.scene: A shelf of brightly wrapped biscuits and ready meals in a shop
beats.summary: Diets high in ultra-processed food are usually low in fibre; some additives are being studied, but effects in humans are still unclear.

beats.scene: A fizzy drink and a slice of cake beside a bowl of lentils
beats.summary: Diets high in sugar and fat and low in fibre are linked with a less varied set of microbes, though cause and effect are not settled.

beats.scene: Noah sleeps in bed while cartoon microbes float calmly above his head
beats.summary: Sleep and stress both seem to affect the gut, and the gut seems to affect sleep and stress in return.

beats.scene: Noah rides his bicycle fast up a hill while Ines jogs behind
beats.summary: Regular exercise is linked with a more varied gut community and with healthier bowel movements.

beats.scene: Water pours into a tall glass beside a bowl of bran flakes and prunes
beats.summary: Fibre works best with enough fluid; a lack of water, fibre and movement is a common cause of constipation.

beats.scene: A calendar with a few ticks each week and a small question mark
beats.summary: Healthy bowel habits vary a great deal from person to person; what matters is what is normal for you and any lasting change.

beats.scene: A red warning sign beside a doctor's door in a clinic corridor
beats.summary: See a doctor, not a diet book, for blood in the stool, black stools, unexplained weight loss, ongoing pain or a lasting change in bowel habits.

beats.scene: A dietitian talks to a person at a desk with a plate model
beats.summary: Some people with bowel conditions, such as irritable bowel syndrome, need a personal plan from a doctor or registered dietitian.

beats.scene: A coloured cleanse drink and a postal test kit on a table
beats.summary: Gut cleanses, detox teas and home stool tests that promise a personal diet have weak evidence, and the body already clears waste.

beats.scene: A baby sleeps in a cot while a parent holds a bottle
beats.summary: A baby's microbes begin to form at birth, and a baby's diet should follow advice from a doctor or health visitor.

beats.scene: Noah holds a bowl of porridge topped with seeds, berries and yoghurt
beats.summary: Noah builds a gut-friendly breakfast with oats, seeds, fruit and yoghurt.

beats.scene: Noah opens a lunch box of bean salad and brown rice on a bench
beats.summary: Noah packs a lunch of bean salad with grains, vegetables and herbs for the road.

beats.scene: Noah and Ines cook a pot of lentil stew in a small kitchen
beats.summary: Noah cooks a lentil and vegetable stew with onions and garlic for dinner.

beats.scene: Noah stops beside a fruit stall and picks up a banana and nuts
beats.summary: Snacks for a courier on the road: fruit, nuts, a boiled egg and a piece of wholemeal bread.

beats.scene: Noah scans a menu at a busy street cafe while a waiter waits
beats.summary: Eating out can still be gut-friendly: choose beans, vegetables, whole grains and a side salad when you can.

beats.scene: Noah counts coins into a small purse beside a shopping list
beats.summary: Gut-friendly food can be cheap: dried beans, oats, frozen vegetables, cabbage and carrots.

beats.scene: Noah stands at Ines's door after six weeks, smiling beside his bicycle
beats.summary: After six weeks Noah feels lighter, though Ines says everybody's results will differ and a feeling is not proof.

beats.scene: Ines stands at a whiteboard covered in question marks and a gut drawing
beats.summary: Ines says that much about the microbiome is still unknown, and good science means admitting what we do not know.

beats.scene: Noah and Ines sit on a bench at sunset with a bicycle
beats.summary: This book is general information and is not medical advice; ask a doctor or dietitian about your own health.

B1B2: Noah rides a bicycle through the city all day, and he usually eats a quick sandwich at a red light. Lately he has started to wonder what all this fast food is doing inside his body.

His neighbour Ines is a microbiologist, which means she studies tiny living things called microbes. She laughs when Noah asks about his stomach and says that the real story is much bigger and stranger.
Ines draws the gut as a long tube that runs through the body. It is several metres long, and food takes many hours to travel all the way through it.
Most of the microbes live in the large intestine, the last part of the gut. By recent estimates, the body holds about as many microbes as it has human cells.
All the microbes living in and on a body are called the microbiome. Everyone has a different mix, a bit like a fingerprint, and it changes over time.
Noah worries that microbes mean germs, but Ines explains that most gut microbes are harmless or helpful. A healthy crowd of them even helps to keep the harmful germs away.
Gut microbes help us to digest food that we cannot digest by ourselves. They make some vitamins, and they also help to train the immune system.
The gut and the brain send messages to each other through nerves, hormones and the immune system. Early research asks whether gut microbes affect mood, but much is still unknown.
The microbes in the gut need food too, and they live mostly on the parts of our meals that we cannot digest. The most important of these parts, by far, is fibre.
Fibre is the part of plant foods that our bodies cannot digest. Soluble fibre dissolves in water and becomes gel-like, while insoluble fibre stays rough and adds bulk.
When microbes ferment fibre, they make substances called short-chain fatty acids. These feed the cells that line the large intestine, and they may also help to calm inflammation.
Many national guides advise adults to eat about thirty grams of fibre a day. In many countries, most adults eat well below that amount.
Noah writes down everything he eats for three days and counts the fibre using food labels. He discovers that he eats far less than the guides suggest.

Ines warns Noah not to change everything overnight, because a gut that is used to little fibre may protest. Adding fibre slowly over several weeks, and drinking enough water, gives the gut time to adjust.
When microbes ferment fibre, they make gases, so a little extra wind is normal at first. Most people pass wind many times a day, and it usually settles down as the gut adapts.
Beans and lentils are rich in fibre and contain protein, and they are cheap. Start with small portions, and rinse tinned beans well, so the gut can adjust.
Whole grains such as oats, barley and brown rice keep their outer layers, so they keep more fibre. Oats and barley also contain beta-glucan, a fibre that microbes can ferment.
Fruit and vegetables bring fibre to every meal, as well as water and vitamins. Eating the skins, when they are clean and safe, adds more, and each kind feeds different microbes.
Nuts and seeds add fibre, protein and healthy fats to meals. Grinding or soaking seeds can make them easier to digest, but nut allergies can be serious.
Different microbes prefer different foods, so a varied diet feeds a more varied community. Eating the same few plants every day leaves many microbes hungry.
A large survey found that people who ate more than thirty kinds of plant a week had a more varied gut community. People who ate ten or fewer had a less varied one, but this is a link and not proof.
Noah starts a chart on his fridge to count the different plants that he eats in a week. Herbs, spices, nuts, seeds, beans and grains all count, so the numbers grow faster than he expected.
In general, a gut with many different kinds of microbes is linked with better health. Ines compares it to a rainforest, which can survive trouble better than a field of one crop.
Prebiotics are types of fibre that help friendly microbes to grow. They are found in onions, garlic, leeks, oats and slightly green bananas.

When starchy foods such as potatoes, rice and pasta are cooked and then cooled, some of their starch becomes resistant to digestion. Microbes in the large intestine can then ferment this starch, and it acts like fibre.

Colourful plants contain natural substances called polyphenols, and so do tea, cocoa and olive oil. Gut microbes can change them into other substances, and early research suggests that these may help health.
Fermented foods are made with the help of microbes, and they include yoghurt, kefir, kimchi, sauerkraut and miso. Some of these still contain living microbes when you eat them.
A small university study asked healthy adults to eat more fermented foods for ten weeks. Their gut microbes became more varied than before, but the study was small.
Probiotic pills contain living microbes, but the evidence for them is mixed. Some help with particular conditions, and a doctor or dietitian can say if you might need one.
Noah tries to make sauerkraut at home from cabbage and salt. Ines tells him to use very clean jars, and to throw it away if it smells bad or grows mould.
Antibiotics save lives, but they kill helpful microbes as well as harmful ones. Take them only when a doctor prescribes them, and follow the instructions carefully.
Many ready meals and snacks contain very little fibre, so the microbes get little to eat. Some additives are being studied, but their effects in people are still unclear.
Diets high in sugar and fat and low in fibre are linked with a less varied set of gut microbes. Scientists have not settled how much of this is cause and how much is effect.
Poor sleep and high stress seem to affect the gut, and the gut seems to affect sleep and stress in return. Research on this is still growing, and none of it is certain.
Regular exercise is linked with a more varied gut community and with healthy bowel movements. Noah already rides all day, so he is ahead in this at least.
Fibre works best with enough fluid, and a lack of water, fibre and movement can cause constipation. Drinking regularly through the day is a simple habit.
Healthy bowel habits vary a lot, from several times a day to a few times a week. What matters is what is normal for you, and any lasting change.
Some signs need a doctor and not a new diet. They include blood in the stool, black stools, weight loss that you cannot explain, ongoing pain, or a lasting change in bowel habits.
Some people have bowel conditions, such as irritable bowel syndrome, and some foods may make them feel worse. A doctor or a registered dietitian can make a plan for them.
Gut cleanses and detox teas have no good evidence, and the body already clears its own waste. Home stool tests that promise a personal diet are not yet reliable.
A baby's microbiome begins to form at birth and changes quickly in the first years. A baby's food should follow the advice of a doctor or health visitor.
Noah's new breakfast is porridge with seeds, berries and a spoonful of yoghurt. It takes five minutes to make, and it already contains four different plants.
Noah packs a lunch of cold brown rice, mixed beans, chopped carrots and fresh herbs. It is cheap and easy to carry, and it also contains resistant starch.
In the evening, Noah cooks a stew from red lentils, onions, garlic, carrots and tomatoes. The onions and garlic are prebiotics, and the whole pot costs very little.
Noah's snacks are now an apple, a banana, a handful of nuts or a piece of wholemeal bread with peanut butter. All of them fit easily in the bag of a courier.
When Noah eats out, he looks for dishes with beans, vegetables or whole grains. A side salad or a bowl of soup also adds plants to his day.
Gut-friendly food does not have to be expensive for ordinary families. Dried beans, oats, carrots, cabbage and frozen vegetables are some of the cheapest foods in the shop.
After six weeks, Noah says he feels lighter and has more energy. Ines is pleased, but she reminds him that results differ, and that a feeling is not proof.
Ines tells Noah how much is still unknown about the microbiome. She says that good science means admitting what we do not know, and that fibre and variety are safe bets.
This book is general information and is not medical advice. If you have a health condition, an allergy, a pregnancy or a child to feed, ask a doctor or a registered dietitian first.
C1C2: Noah spends ten hours a day delivering parcels by bicycle, and he eats whatever is fastest, usually a sandwich or a bag of crisps at a red traffic light. Lately he has noticed that he feels heavy and sleepy in the afternoons, and he has started to wonder what all this hurried eating is doing inside his body. He decides that the person to ask is his neighbour Ines, who works at the university and always seems to know the answer.

Ines is a microbiologist at the university, which means that she spends her days studying living things too small to see without a microscope. When Noah asks her about his tired afternoons, she laughs, makes two cups of tea and says that the real story begins in a place he has probably never thought about. She also warns him that she will only tell him what science knows, and will say plainly when it does not.

Ines draws a long, winding tube on the whiteboard and explains that this is the gut, which runs from the mouth all the way through the body. It is several metres long when stretched out, and food takes many hours, even a day or more, to make the whole journey. Noah looks at the drawing and realises that he has been treating it as little more than a bin.

Most of the microbes in the gut live in the large intestine, the last and widest part of the tube, and there are trillions of them. People used to say that microbes outnumbered human cells ten to one, but more careful counting suggests that the numbers are about equal. Noah says that this is still a rather large crowd to be sharing his body with.

The microbiome is the collective name for the whole community of microorganisms living in and on a body, and the greatest share of it inhabits the gut. Each person carries a distinctive mixture, rather like a fingerprint, and it shifts over time with age, diet, medicine and the places where a person has lived. Ines says that no two people share exactly the same community, not even identical twins, although twins come surprisingly close.

Noah worries that microbes must mean germs, and Ines tells him that only a small number of species cause illness and that most of the microbes in a healthy gut are harmless or even helpful. A thriving crowd of friendly microbes takes up space and food, and so it can make life difficult for the harmful ones that arrive by accident. It is like a full café, she says, where there are simply no free tables for troublemakers.

Gut microbes do several jobs for their host, which is the person they live in. They break down parts of food that human digestion cannot manage, they make some vitamins, including vitamin K and some of the B group, and they help to train the immune system to tell friends from enemies. Noah realises that he is hosting a team of tiny workers who have never asked for a pay rise.

The gut and the brain are in constant conversation, sending messages along nerves and through hormones and immune signals. Scientists are studying whether gut microbes can influence mood, stress and sleep, and the early results are fascinating, but most of them come from animals or small studies and cannot yet be turned into advice. Ines says that she would love to tell him more, but she would rather be honest than exciting.

The microbes in the large intestine need to eat, and what they feed on is whatever reaches them from a meal that the person has already digested. Most of it is fibre and similar carbohydrates that the human body has no tools to break down, so for the microbes a plant-rich meal is a feast and a plate of white bread is a very small snack. Noah says, with a grin, that he had never before thought of himself as a kind of restaurant.

Fibre is the tough part of plant foods that our digestive juices cannot break down, and it is found in vegetables, fruit, beans, whole grains, nuts and seeds, but not in meat, fish, eggs or dairy products. Scientists often divide it into soluble fibre, which dissolves in water and turns gel-like, and insoluble fibre, which stays rough and adds bulk, and most plant foods contain a mixture of both. Ines says that this is a rough division, since real foods are always more complicated.

When the microbes ferment fibre, they produce substances called short-chain fatty acids, and one of them, butyrate, is a favourite fuel for the cells that line the large intestine. These substances may also help to calm inflammation in the body, although much of the evidence comes from laboratory work and animals and is still being tested in people. Ines draws a small flame on the whiteboard and says that fibre becomes fuel, but not in the way that most people expect.

Many national guides advise adults to eat around thirty grams of fibre a day, although the exact figure varies a little from country to country. Surveys in many countries show that most adults eat considerably less than that, often by a third or more, and Ines suspects that Noah is no exception. Noah cheerfully admits that he has no idea how much he is eating and agrees to find out.

Noah writes down everything that he eats for three days and checks the labels to count his fibre, which takes longer than he expected. The result is a surprise, since most of his meals are made of white bread, cheese, chips and sweet drinks, and his total is far below the target that Ines mentioned. He is not ashamed, because Ines assures him that she has seen this result many times, and she says that it is easy to fix.

Ines warns Noah not to change everything overnight, because a gut that is used to very little fibre can protest loudly when a lot arrives at once. Adding a little more each few days over several weeks gives the microbes time to adapt, and drinking enough water helps the fibre to do its work without causing discomfort. Noah promises to be patient, which for a man who lives on a bicycle is quite a commitment.

Fermentation makes gas, so a little extra wind is a normal result when a person begins to eat more fibre, and it usually settles down after a few weeks as the microbes adapt. Most healthy people pass wind many times a day, whether they admit it or not, and Ines says that a gut which never produced any would be a gut with very hungry microbes. Noah tries not to laugh in the middle of the laboratory corridor, and fails.

Beans, lentils and chickpeas are some of the best foods for gut microbes, since they are rich in fibre and in special carbohydrates that the microbes love, and they are also cheap and rich in protein. Ines suggests that Noah begin with a few spoonfuls, rinse tinned beans under a tap, and increase the portion gradually until his gut stops complaining. Dried red kidney beans, she adds, must be soaked and boiled hard for at least ten minutes before they are safe to eat.

Whole grains keep the outer layers of the seed, where much of the fibre and many minerals are found, and refined grains such as white bread and white rice have lost most of it. Oats and barley contain a type of fibre called beta-glucan, which is sticky and easily fermented by microbes, and Ines says that a bowl of porridge is one of the simplest gut-friendly breakfasts. Noah swaps his white toast for porridge, and discovers that it keeps him full until lunch.

Fruit and vegetables bring fibre, water and many natural plant substances to a meal, and the skins and seeds of many of them, once they have been washed, are especially rich in fibre. Different vegetables contain different kinds of fibre, so a mixed plate feeds a wider range of microbes than a plate of just one or two. Noah begins to keep carrots and apples in his delivery bag instead of crisps.

Nuts and seeds are small, but they bring fibre, protein and healthy fats to a meal, and a spoonful of seeds sprinkled onto porridge or soup is an easy way to add variety. Seeds such as flax are easier to digest when they are ground or soaked, and anybody with a nut or seed allergy must of course avoid them completely, since such allergies can be dangerous. Noah has no allergy at all, so he happily enjoys the crunch of every new seed that he tries.

Different microbes prefer different fibres, which means that a varied diet feeds a more varied community, while eating the same few plants every day leaves many species hungry and in decline. Ines compares the gut to a garden, where a single crop is fragile and a mixture of plants is tougher, and she tells Noah that variety is as important as quantity. Noah looks at his usual shopping list and realises that it contains hardly any plants at all.

Ines shows Noah the results of a large citizen-science survey, in which thousands of volunteers shared samples and described their diets. People who ate more than thirty different kinds of plant a week had a more varied set of gut microbes than people who ate ten or fewer, but this is only a link. Thirty is a handy target rather than a magic number, and Noah says that he would be happy with fifteen to begin with.

Noah sticks a chart to his fridge and puts a tick next to every kind of plant that he eats during the week. Herbs, spices, nuts, seeds, beans and grains all count, and so a tin of mixed beans, a pinch of cumin and a handful of walnuts quickly push his score upwards. By the end of the first week he has reached twelve, which is double what he had eaten the week before.

A gut with many different kinds of microbes is generally linked with better health, although scientists are still working out how much the variety is a cause of good health and how much it is a result. Ines compares a varied gut to a rainforest, which can survive a storm or a pest far better than a field that contains only one kind of crop. Noah agrees that he would rather have a rainforest than a field of wheat.

Prebiotics are types of fibre and similar substances that selectively feed friendly microbes, and they are found in onions, garlic, leeks, asparagus, oats and slightly green bananas. Ines explains that the word is easily confused with probiotics, which are living microbes in food or pills, and she writes both words on the whiteboard to help Noah remember. Prebiotics, she says, are the food that the microbes enjoy, whereas probiotics are the guests who arrive hoping to be fed.

When starchy foods such as potatoes, rice and pasta are cooked and then allowed to cool, some of their starch becomes resistant to digestion, so it passes through to the large intestine where microbes can ferment it. Slightly green bananas and many beans also contain resistant starch, and Ines says that a cold potato salad is therefore a better friend to the gut than the same potato eaten hot and mashed. Rice must be cooled quickly and kept in the fridge, she adds, since it can carry harmful bacteria if left out.

Colourful plants, tea, cocoa, olive oil and berries contain thousands of natural substances called polyphenols, and only a small part of them is absorbed in the early part of the gut. The rest reaches the microbes, who change them into other substances, and early research suggests that some of these may help health, although the studies are still young. Ines puts a purple cabbage on her desk and says that a vegetable is a whole chemistry set.

Fermented foods have been made for thousands of years by letting microbes change milk, vegetables or beans, and they include yoghurt, kefir, kimchi, sauerkraut and miso. Some of them still contain living microbes when they are eaten, and Ines says that eating them is an easy way to meet new microbes, although whether those microbes stay for long in a grown-up gut is still being studied. Noah buys a jar of kimchi at the market and tries it with his rice.

Ines tells Noah about a small study at a university in the United States, in which healthy adults were asked to eat more fermented foods for ten weeks. Their gut microbes became more varied by the end of the study, and some signs of inflammation fell, but the group was small and the results need to be confirmed by larger trials. For now, she says, fermented food looks promising, and it happens to taste very good with rice.

Probiotic pills and drinks contain particular living microbes, and Ines explains that the evidence for them is mixed, since some strains help with certain conditions but others do little at all. The microbes usually do not stay for long after a person stops taking them, and they are no replacement for a varied diet. Anyone who is tempted to buy one for a particular problem should ask a doctor or registered dietitian first, so Noah puts the bottle back on the pharmacy shelf.

Noah decides to make his own sauerkraut by squeezing shredded cabbage with salt in a very clean glass jar until its own juice covers it. Ines tells him to keep it below the liquid, to leave it at room temperature for a week or two, and to throw it away if it smells rotten or grows mould, since fermenting is simple but hygiene matters. After ten days he tastes it, makes a face and then, to his surprise, takes another forkful.

When Noah's sister catches a nasty infection, her doctor prescribes antibiotics, and Ines is quick to say that these medicines save lives and must be taken exactly as instructed. They do, however, kill helpful microbes as well as harmful ones, and the gut usually recovers within weeks or months, so antibiotics should be used only when a doctor prescribes them, never for a cold or flu. Eating plenty of varied plant foods afterwards, Ines suggests, is a sensible way to help the recovery.

Diets that are high in ultra-processed foods are usually low in fibre, and so they leave the microbes with very little to eat, which is probably the main problem. Some additives in such foods are being studied, and experiments in mice suggest that a few may disturb the gut, but the effects in humans are still unclear and Ines refuses to say more than that. Noah gives his crisps a long, thoughtful look and eats only half of the bag.

Diets that are high in sugar and fat and low in fibre are linked with a less varied set of gut microbes, and animal studies suggest that this may be partly a cause and not just a result. Scientists have not settled how much of the link in people is cause and how much is effect, so Ines says that the safest summary is that fibre-rich diets seem to suit the gut better. Noah nods slowly, glances at his cake and adds another spoonful of lentils to his plate.

Poor sleep and heavy stress seem to affect the gut, and the gut in turn seems to affect sleep and mood, so the link runs in both directions. Research in this area is growing quickly, but none of it is certain enough yet to give firm rules, and Ines says that going to bed at a regular time is good advice for nearly everybody. Noah, who has always gone to bed at midnight and woken up grumpy, makes a small and sincere promise to try an earlier hour.

Regular exercise is linked with a more varied set of gut microbes and with more regular bowel movements, although it is hard to separate the effect of exercise from the other habits of people who exercise. Noah already rides his bicycle for ten hours a day, and Ines points out, with a smile, that the legs of a courier may be well ahead of his gut. He laughs and says that at last he has found one thing he is doing right.

Fibre soaks up water as it moves through the gut, and it works best when a person drinks enough fluid, since a lack of water, fibre and movement is a common cause of constipation. Drinking regularly through the day is a simple habit, and Noah, who spends his working hours on a bicycle in the sun, notices that he often forgets to drink anything at all until the evening. He fills a bottle, fastens it firmly to the frame of his bicycle and resolves to sip at every red light.

Noah asks Ines how often he should go to the toilet, and she explains that healthy bowel habits vary a great deal, from several times a day to a few times a week. There is no single correct number, and what matters most is what is normal for each person and whether it changes for a long time, in which case it is wise to talk to a doctor. Noah is relieved to hear that nobody is grading him on this particular subject.

Ines becomes serious and tells Noah that some signs need a doctor and not a new diet, and that no book, including a book about food, should be used to treat them. They include blood in the stool, black stools, weight loss that cannot be explained, pain that does not go away and a change in bowel habits that lasts for several weeks. Noah promises that he will never ignore any of these, and Ines says that this is the most important thing she will tell him.

Some people have bowel conditions, such as irritable bowel syndrome or inflammatory bowel disease, and for them certain high-fibre foods can sometimes make symptoms worse and not better. Such people should ask a doctor or registered dietitian for a personal plan, and they should not cut out whole groups of food on their own, particularly gluten, before they have been tested for conditions like coeliac disease. Noah's friend Rafi has such a plan, and Noah is glad that he does.

Noah sees advertisements for gut cleanses, detox teas and home test kits that promise to design a personal diet from a sample, and he asks Ines whether he should buy one. She tells him that cleanses and detox teas have no good evidence behind them, since the gut already clears its own waste, and that tests of this kind are not yet reliable enough to guide a diet. He decides to keep his money for a large bag of beans, which Ines says is the wisest purchase of all.

A baby's microbiome begins to form at birth and changes quickly over the first few years of life, shaped by feeding, family and the environment. Noah's sister has a baby, and Ines says that a baby's food should follow the advice of a doctor or a health visitor and not the advice of a book about adult diets. Adult plans of fibre and fermentation, she adds, are not designed for the very young.

Noah's new breakfast is a bowl of porridge topped with a spoonful of seeds, some frozen berries and a little plain yoghurt, and it takes only five minutes to make. It already counts as four or five different plants before he has left the kitchen, and it keeps him full until well after the first deliveries of the day. He tells Ines that, for the first time, he has looked forward to breakfast.

For his lunch box, Noah mixes cold brown rice with tinned mixed beans, chopped carrots, spring onions and fresh herbs, and he dresses it with olive oil and lemon. It is cheap and easy to carry in a bicycle bag, and the cooked and cooled rice adds resistant starch to the fibre of the beans and vegetables. He eats it on a park bench and, for once, he does not feel sleepy afterwards.

For dinner, Noah cooks a big pot of stew from lentils, onions, garlic, carrots and tinned tomatoes, with a pinch of cumin and a handful of spinach at the end. The onions and garlic are prebiotics, the lentils are rich in fibre, and the whole pot costs very little and makes four portions. Ines tastes it and declares that her lab could not have designed a better meal.

Noah's snacks are now an apple, a banana, a handful of nuts or a slice of wholemeal bread with peanut butter, and all of them fit comfortably into the bag of a courier who is always on the move. Each one adds a little fibre and a new kind of plant to his weekly count, and none needs a plate, a fork or a table. He has not bought a bag of crisps for two weeks, and he is surprised at how little he misses them.

Noah does not want to give up eating out with friends, so he learns to look for dishes with beans, vegetables or whole grains. When the main course has few plants, he adds a side salad or a bowl of soup. Ines tells him that one meal never makes or breaks a diet, and that the pattern across many weeks is what counts.

Noah worries that this way of eating will be expensive, but Ines shows him that dried beans, lentils, oats, cabbage, carrots, frozen vegetables and tinned tomatoes are some of the cheapest foods in any shop. Cooking at home from such ingredients usually costs far less than takeaways and ready meals, and the money Noah saves on crisps and sweet drinks pays for a jar of kimchi. By the end of the week his wallet is surprisingly heavier, and his shopping bag is a good deal more colourful.

After six weeks, Noah tells Ines that he feels lighter, that his afternoons are no longer sleepy and that his bicycle seems to go uphill more easily. Ines is delighted, but she reminds him that everyone responds differently, that other changes in his life may have helped, and that a good feeling is encouraging without being proof. Noah says that this is the most scientific thing anyone has ever said to him, and he thanks her anyway.

Ines tells Noah that, in spite of all the excitement, a great deal about the microbiome is still unknown, including which microbes matter most and how far a person can change their own community. She says that good science means admitting what we do not know, but that eating more fibre and more variety is a safe bet that is supported by many kinds of evidence. Noah says that he can live with a safe bet, especially one that tastes as good as a lentil stew.

That evening, Noah and Ines sit on a bench with a bicycle between them and agree that feeding the gut is mostly a matter of eating more plants, and more kinds of plants. This book gives general information only and is not medical advice, so anyone with a health condition, an allergy, a pregnancy, a child to feed or a medicine to take should ask a doctor or registered dietitian first. For everyone else, the next step is small and friendly, which is to add one new plant to tomorrow's meal.
